items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we want to find the point of intersection between the two lines [MATH: y = x + 2] and [MATH: y = 2x + 1.] A sketch of both lines and the point of intersection [MATH: P] is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c75353a3cf3587d62fa4c9b923d4fe51]

Content:
The point [MATH: P] consists of the coordinates [MATH: (x,y)] that satisfy both equations [MATH: y=x+2] and [MATH: y=2x+1.] So, to find the coordinates of [MATH: P] we need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:
[MATH: {y = x + 2; y = 2x + 1]

Content:
We can solve this system by substitution. Substituting the first equation [MATH: y=x+2] into the second equation [MATH: y=2x+1] gives an equation that we can solve for [MATH: x\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: x + 2|= 2x + 1; x + 1|= 2x; 1|= x]

Content:
This is the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the point of intersection. To find the [MATH: y]-coordinate, we substitute [MATH: x = 1] back into one of the equations, say [MATH: y=x+2,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: y|= x + 2; = 1 + 2; = 3]

Content:
Therefore, the solution to the system is [MATH: x=1, \, y=3.] So, the point of intersection has the coordinates [MATH: (1,3).]

The point of intersection consists of the coordinates [MATH: (x,y)] that satisfy both equations [MATH: y=5x+3] and [MATH: y=x-1.] So, we need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

[MATH: {y = 5x + 3; y = x − 1]

We will use the substitution method to solve the system. Substituting the first equation [MATH: y=5x+3] into the second equation [MATH: y=x-1] gives an equation that we can solve for [MATH: x\mathbin{:}] [MATH: 5x + 3|= x − 1; 5x|= x − 4; 4x|= − 4; x|= − 1]

This is the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the point of intersection. To find the [MATH: y]-coordinate, we substitute [MATH: x = -1] back into one of the equations, say [MATH: y=x-1,] as follows:

[MATH: y|= x − 1; = − 1 − 1; = − 2]

Therefore, the solution to the system is [MATH: x=-1, \, y=-2.] So, the coordinates of the intersection point are [MATH: (-1,-2).]

sections.normalized_html:
We need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

[MATH: {x + 2y = 1; 2x − y = 7]

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the second equation by [MATH: 2,] then we will get a [MATH: -2y] term that can cancel with the [MATH: 2y] term in the first equation:

[MATH: {x + 2y = 1; 2x − y = 7||× 2]

Adding the two equations eliminates the [MATH: y]-variable and allows us to solve for [MATH: x\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: x + 2y|= 1; 4x − 2y|= 14; (x + 4x)|= (1 + 14); 5x|= 15; x|= 3]

Finally, we can substitute [MATH: x=3] into the equation [MATH: x+2y=1] to solve for [MATH: y\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: x + 2y|= 1; 3 + 2y|= 1; 2y|= − 2; y|= − 1]

Therefore, the solution to the system is [MATH: x=3, \, y=-1.] So the coordinates of the point of intersection are [MATH: (3,-1).]

sections.normalized_html:
Since [MATH: (b,-4)] is the point of intersection of the two lines, the values [MATH: x=b, \, y=-4] must solve the following system:

[MATH: {y = − 3x + a; y = x − 1]

We substitute [MATH: x=b, \, y=-4] to obtain a new system:

[MATH: {− 4 = − 3b + a; − 4 = b − 1]

In the second equation, we can solve for [MATH: b\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: − 4|= b − 1; − 3|= b]

Then, we can substitute [MATH: b=-3] into the first equation and solve for [MATH: a\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: − 4|= − 3b + a; − 4|= − 3(− 3) + a; − 4|= 9 + a; − 13|= a]

Therefore, [MATH: a = -13] and [MATH: b = -3.]
